world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Welsh Romani (wels1246) is not in the catalog. The single Glottolog title-keyword item, Murphy 2016 'Evolutionary monkey oscillomics' (Theoretical Linguistics), is a neuro-oscillation commentary with no bearing on Romani or stress (Crossref record saved); its attachment to wels1246 is spurious.org, Open Library search-inside, Crossref, Semantic Scholar and HathiTrust catalog APIs. The primary source, Sampson 1926 The Dialect of the Gypsies of Wales (stress pp. 23-28), has a public-domain HathiTrust full-view scan but is Cloudflare-blocked from our machine and from web lookups, Google Books is 403/quota-0, and no archive.org or Open Library copy exists: HIGH priority to acquire from a US IP or a library. First-hand statements actually read and verified on page images: Sampson 1909 JGLS NS 3 p. 17 fn. 2 (demonstratives oxytone when substantival, paroxytone when adjectival), Sampson 1908-09 JGLS NS 2 p. 146 fn. 6 (imperatives of -d/-t stems stressed on the stem) and p. 55 fn. (clitic group stressed on the penult), and Sampson 1922 JGLS 3rd ser. 1 p. 91 (accent written only when chief stress is not on the first syllable). Matras 2002 §4.2.6 (snippets via Open Library, saved) summarizes Sampson 1926 as: nouns/adjectives final-stressed in predicative use, initial elsewhere; demonstratives penultimate attributive vs final pronominal; optional retraction from final stress (ákaj < akáj).org) — accented text, silent on rules; Nature 1926 Sampson letter — first sentence only, nothing on stress. new_statements.translation_language: English (Welsh Romani examples; diacritics transcribed from the page image as closely as the OCR/PNG allow)
new_statements.rule_in_words: No single general rule is stated in any source opened. What the first-hand pages show: Sampson's Welsh Romani texts carry marked (mostly final) stress on the great majority of inherited polysyllables, i.e. the conservative Romani 'grammatical' stress on the last syllable of the inflected word (Layer-1 endings), while words left unmarked - mainly English/Welsh loans and short items - have first-syllable stress by convention; stress is grammatically conditioned in at least two categories (demonstratives: final when pronominal, penultimate when attributive; -d/-t imperatives: stem-stressed). Matras's second-hand summary of Sampson 1926 (nouns/adjectives final when predicative, initial elsewhere) points to a partial retraction toward initial stress that the 1909 texts do not obviously show; the conflict cannot be resolved without Sampson 1926: 23-28.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Demonstratives: oxytone when substantival, paroxytone when adjectival (1909: 17 n. 2). Imperative singular of -d/-t verb stems in -de/-te carries the accent on the stem syllable (1908-09: 146 n. 6). 'Accent of rapid speech' contractions (mār'na for maréna) (1909: 17 n. 1). Per Matras 2002: 63-64 (second-hand, from Sampson 1926: 23-8) nouns and adjectives take final stress when predicative but initial stress elsewhere; vowel lengthening optional in Welsh Romani.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from Sampson's phonetically accented text transcriptions of Matthew Wood's tales (Tal-y-Llyn / Bala, North Wales, recorded from 1894) and his transcription conventions; the demonstrative rule is syntactically conditioned (substantival vs. adjectival use). The general accent rule is in Sampson 1926 pp. 23-28, not in hand.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand material is Sampson's record of the Kāle dialect of the Abram Wood clan (Matthew Wood and kin, Tal-y-Llyn/Bala, Merioneth), recorded 1894-1920s = wels1246 itself (Matras 2002 calls it 'Welsh Romani or the Kaale dialect'). Not to be confused with Angloromani (angl1239, rme) or the older inflected English Romani of Smart & Crofton 1875, whose accent notes (final-syllable accentuation among older English Gypsies) turned up in the same JGLS volumes.

Journal of the Gypsy Lore Society, New Series 3(1): 17-19 — p. 17 fn. 2; read together with Sampson (1922) On the Writing of Romani, JGLS Third Series 1: 91 (accent-marking convention) and Sampson (1908-09) JGLS New Series 2: 146 fn. 6.

new_statements.reading: Welsh Romani has lexically/grammatically placed (not fixed) word stress in Sampson's own first-hand notes: demonstratives are final-stressed in pronominal/predicative use and penultimate-stressed in attributive use; -d/-t verb stems form stem-stressed imperatives; and his transcription convention leaves stress unmarked only when it falls on the first syllable, so initial stress is the unmarked default in his texts and non-initial (mostly final, the conservative Romani pattern) stress is marked. This matches the secondary summary in Matras 2002 §4.2.6 of Sampson 1926: 23-28 (nouns/adjectives final-stressed in predicative use, initial elsewhere; demonstratives penultimate attributive vs final pronominal; optional retraction ákaj < akáj). The general rule statement itself (Sampson 1926 pp. 23-28) was not readable from our machine; these footnotes are the best first-hand statements actually read.

sources.note: p. 17 fn. 2 (first-hand, Sampson): demonstrative pronouns take oxytone accent when used substantivally, paroxytone when used adjectivally (okóva mūrš vs. oková sī ō mūrš). The accented text on the same page shows final stress marked on most inherited words (givéskō, guruvá, ṗalá, devél, gonó, kirčíma, lovína, bakaré, Akavá) and unmarked (=initial) stress on loans/short words.

sources.tag: read: notes on stress
sources.quote: At the suggestion of the Editor I here supply the characters used by myself in writing Welsh Romani ... Quantity is marked in the case of long vowels only, and accent only on the syllable taking the chief stress when other than the first. [fn. 2:] In unstressed syllables ending in a vowel, final ā, ē, ī, ō are generally only half-long ... In Welsh Romani I use the former.
sources.note: Transcription convention, not a rule statement: Sampson leaves the accent unmarked when chief stress is on the first syllable, so unaccented words in his Welsh Romani texts are initial-stressed and all non-initial (typically final) stress is marked. Implies initial stress is his default for the language as written.

sources.quote: 4.2.6 Stress / Early Romani had word-level grammatical stress, which is preserved in con[servative dialects] ... In the pre-European ('thematic') component, stress is on the [final syllable] ... frequent shift away from fi-nal stress, and optionally in Welsh Romani (ákaj < akáj 'here') ... For Welsh Romani, Sampson (1926: 23-8) mentions that nouns and adjectives take final stress when used in predicative constructions, but initial stress elsewhere, and that demonstratives have penultimate stress in attributive positions but final stress in pronominal function
